text: Instead of etching a qubit into a chip, trapped-ion hardware takes a single atom, strips an electron off it, and suspends it in mid-air with electromagnetic fields. It's a genuinely different engineering approach from the superconducting chips in Chapter 1, with its own physics, its own equipment, and its own failure modes.

A trapped-ion qubit starts with a single atom of a chosen element — ytterbium, calcium, or barium are common — that's had one electron removed, leaving a net positive charge. That charge is the whole point: a neutral atom can't be grabbed by electric fields, but a charged ion can. The qubit's two states are encoded in two long-lived internal energy levels, chosen specifically because they resist decay and are relatively insensitive to stray fields. Nothing here is fabricated — every ion of the same species is, by nature, identical to every other one, which sidesteps the chip-to-chip manufacturing variation superconducting qubits have to fight.

This is a real ion trap chip, mounted inside its vacuum enclosure. The gold-plated electrodes you see are what confine and address the ions, with wiring running out to room-temperature control electronics — this whole assembly sits in ultra-high vacuum so stray gas molecules don't knock the ion out of its quantum state.

A charged particle can't simply be parked in space with a static field, so trapped-ion systems use a Paul trap: electrodes carrying a fast-oscillating radio-frequency voltage, plus static voltages, that together create an effective bowl-shaped trap. Load more than one ion, and they don't clump together — they repel each other through the Coulomb force, settling into a stable, evenly-spaced linear chain. And before any gate can run reliably, that chain has to be cooled, starting with Doppler cooling, where an off-resonance laser saps kinetic energy from the ions on average, bringing the chain toward its quantum mechanical motional ground state.
Next lesson: how gates actually get applied to this chain. There are no wires running to each ion — every single-qubit and two-qubit gate on this hardware is done with laser light.
